title: Unity vs. Godot for AI-assisted game development — is switching worth it?
author: RealMiniBU
selftext:
Hey everyone!

I've been developing my game in Unity for about six months now, and I've already reached the pre-alpha stage with a playable build and most of the core mechanics implemented.

My game is a 3D management/strategy simulator. It doesn't involve direct tactical control on a global map. Instead, the gameplay focuses on simulation, management decisions, and interactive progression systems.

The entire game is built in 3D, and I'm aiming for fairly realistic visuals, along with a clean, intuitive, and user-friendly interface.

I'm currently using AI tools to assist with development, mainly Codex with MCP servers and Meshy AI for asset generation.

Here's my question: Would switching from Unity to Godot actually make AI-assisted development more efficient?

I'm particularly interested in how well AI coding agents work with each engine, how easily they can interact with the editor, generate and modify scenes, handle UI development, and work with 3D assets, animations, and VFX.

Since I already have a working pre-alpha in Unity, switching engines would obviously mean a significant amount of extra work.

But if Godot offers substantially better AI integration and a smoother development workflow in the long run, I'd be willing to consider it.

Would you recommend making the switch, or should I stick with Unity and focus on improving my AI development pipeline?

I'd really appreciate hearing from developers who have worked with both engines, especially those using AI agents extensively.

comments.author: TrueSquare_Dev
comments.body:
We build our mobile games in Godot 4 with coding agents, so a few concrete points from the Godot side:

Scenes (.tscn), resources (.tres) and GDScript are all plain text, so an agent can read and edit them directly and you review normal diffs. Godot also runs headless from the command line, so agents can run scripted tests and export builds (including Android) without touching the editor GUI. That combination is the main reason it works well for us.

The weak spots, in our experience: agents are less fluent in GDScript than in C# or Python, and they often mix up Godot 3 and Godot 4 APIs, so pin the version in your instructions. Editing .tscn files by hand can also break node paths or resource IDs, so have the agent load the scene headless to validate after every change. Complex 3D, animation trees and VFX still need a human in the editor.

Six months into a 3D sim with a working Unity pipeline, I would lean toward staying and fixing the specific pain point (domain reload time, for example, can be reduced with the Enter Play Mode options). A switch makes more sense at the start of your next project.

(Written with AI assistance from our studio notes.)
